questions.q: Which protein compartment is preferentially depleted in kwashiorkor compared with marasmus, accounting for hypoalbuminaemia and generalized pitting oedema?
questions.explain: Kwashiorkor is characterized by severe depletion of the visceral protein pool (albumin, transferrin, prealbumin synthesized by the liver), whereas marasmus primarily depletes the somatic protein compartment (skeletal muscle) and subcutaneous fat while preserving serum albumin.

open.q: Which body protein compartment is preferentially depleted in kwashiorkor, leading to hypoalbuminaemia and pitting oedema?

questions.q: Why does marked hepatomegaly with severe diffuse macrovesicular steatosis develop in children with kwashiorkor?
options: Reduced hepatic synthesis of apolipoproteins impairs VLDL triglyceride export from the liver
Excessive dietary intake of saturated triglycerides overwhelms biliary excretion
Hyperinsulinaemia stimulates uncontrolled hepatic glycogen and lipid storage
Autoimmune destruction of hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells blocks chylomicron uptake
questions.explain: Severe dietary protein deficiency impairs hepatic synthesis of apolipoprotein B-100 and other carrier proteins required to package triglycerides into very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), trapping fat inside hepatocytes.

open.q: What biochemical mechanism causes severe fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) in children with kwashiorkor?
accept: Impaired apolipoprotein synthesis reducing hepatic VLDL export
Decreased synthesis of apolipoproteins needed to export triglycerides

questions.q: Which cutaneous abnormality, characterized by alternating zones of hyperpigmentation, desquamation, and hypopigmentation, is classically observed in severe kwashiorkor?
questions.explain: Children with kwashiorkor develop characteristic 'flaky paint' dermatosis on pressure areas and lower limbs, alongside sparse, depigmented, reddish-yellow hair (the 'flag sign' when alternating with normal dark hair bands).

open.q: Name the classic desquamating skin lesion with alternating hyperpigmented and hypopigmented areas seen in kwashiorkor.

questions.q: A 14-month-old Nigerian child brought to an outpatient clinic weighs 54% of expected weight for age, exhibits severe generalized muscle wasting with a wrinkled 'old-man' facies, loss of buccal fat pads, an alert voracious appetite, and complete absence of peripheral oedema. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: Marasmus results from balanced starvation of both calories and protein (<60% expected weight for age), causing extreme somatic muscle and fat wasting, shrunken monkey-like or old-man facies, alert appetite, and no oedema.

open.q: Name the form of severe protein-energy malnutrition characterized by weight under 60% of expected for age, extreme muscle and fat wasting, and absence of oedema.

questions.q: Which morphological change occurs in the small intestinal mucosa of children with severe protein-energy malnutrition and contributes to intractable diarrhoea and malabsorption?
options: Villous atrophy with flattening of the brush border and loss of disaccharidases
Marked elongation and hyperplasia of duodenal Brunner glands
Diffuse transmural granulomatous inflammation with cobblestone mucosa
Metaplastic replacement of enterocytes by keratinizing squamous epithelium
questions.explain: Because intestinal epithelial cells have a rapid turnover rate, protein-energy malnutrition causes marked mucosal thinning, villous blunting/atrophy, reduced mitotic index in crypts, and loss of brush-border lactase and sucrase.

open.q: What structural mucosal lesion develops in the small intestine during severe protein-energy malnutrition, leading to disaccharidase deficiency and malabsorption?

questions.q: During rapid aggressive refeeding of a severely malnourished patient, insulin surges drive extracellular ions into cells, precipitating life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory failure. Which electrolyte disturbance is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
questions.explain: In refeeding syndrome, carbohydrate-induced insulin secretion stimulates cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium for ATP and protein synthesis, causing precipitous hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia.

open.q: Name the hallmark electrolyte abnormality triggered by insulin-mediated cellular uptake during rapid nutritional rehabilitation in refeeding syndrome.

questions.q: What is the earliest clinical symptom of vitamin A (retinol) deficiency?
questions.explain: 11-cis-retinal is an essential prosthetic group of rhodopsin in retinal rod photoreceptors; its depletion impairs dim-light vision first (nyctalopia) before structural ocular surface changes develop.

open.q: What is the earliest clinical symptom of vitamin A deficiency?

questions.q: In vitamin A deficiency, foamy triangular plaques of keratinized squamous debris accumulate on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva. What are these pathognomonic lesions called?
questions.explain: Vitamin A is required to maintain normal mucus-secreting columnar epithelium; deficiency induces squamous metaplasia and keratinization of the conjunctiva (xerophthalmia), producing silvery-white foamy Bitot spots.

open.q: Name the foamy, triangular, keratinized plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva characteristic of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.q: Beyond ocular xerophthalmia and keratomalacia, how does vitamin A deficiency predispose children in low-resource settings to severe respiratory and urinary tract infections?
options: Loss of retinoic-acid signalling causes squamous metaplasia of protective mucosal epithelia
Vitamin A is the sole cofactor for neutrophil myeloperoxidase
Retinol deficiency deletes all B-cell precursors
Vitamin A deficiency paralyses the diaphragm
questions.explain: Retinoic acid regulates epithelial differentiation; its deficiency causes replacement of ciliated, mucus-secreting respiratory epithelium and transitional urothelium by keratinizing squamous epithelium, impairing mucociliary clearance and promoting desquamated keratin niduses for renal stones.

open.q: Which epithelial adaptation occurs in the respiratory and urinary tracts during vitamin A deficiency, predisposing to infection and renal calculi?

questions.q: Why does acute measles infection frequently precipitate sudden blinding keratomalacia in marginally nourished children in Nigeria?
options: Measles damages corneal epithelium and increases vitamin A demand, rapidly depleting marginal stores
Measles converts retinaldehyde into toxic crystals
Measles causes acute PTH suppression and corneal calcification
questions.explain: Measles causes viral keratitis, suppresses hepatic synthesis of retinol-binding protein, and increases metabolic demand for vitamin A, rapidly exhausting borderline liver reserves and triggering corneal ulceration and liquefaction (keratomalacia).

open.q: Why does measles infection frequently precipitate acute keratomalacia and blindness in children with borderline vitamin A stores?
accept: Rapid depletion of hepatic vitamin A stores combined with viral corneal epithelial damage
Depletion of retinol stores and reduced retinol-binding protein synthesis

questions.q: What is the fundamental histological defect in bone caused by vitamin D deficiency in both growing children (rickets) and adults (osteomalacia)?
options: Failure of mineralization of newly formed osteoid matrix
Excessive osteoclastic resorption with normal bone mineralization
Complete absence of osteoblast osteoid synthesis
Replacement of marrow space by dense woven hypermineralized bone
questions.explain: Vitamin D deficiency lowers serum calcium and phosphate, preventing hydroxyapatite crystal deposition in osteoid; consequently, wide seams of unmineralized osteoid accumulate around trabeculae, causing soft, deformed bones.

open.q: What is the core bone mineralization defect underlying both rickets and osteomalacia?

questions.q: Why does rickets produce widening of the wrists, rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, and bowing of weight-bearing long bones, whereas osteomalacia in adults does not?
options: Open growth plates in children develop poorly mineralised, widened cartilage; adult osteomalacia affects bone mineralisation after closure
Rickets is caused by excess calcitonin, whereas osteomalacia is caused by excess PTH
Adults lack osteoblasts capable of producing collagen
Epiphyseal cartilage persists only in the adult axial skeleton
questions.explain: In growing children with open physes, vitamin D deficiency impairs apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes and calcification of the provisional zone of cartilage, producing disorganized, widened epiphyseal growth plates that flare under mechanical load.

open.q: Why do skeletal growth-plate deformities such as the rachitic rosary and widened wrists develop in rickets but not in adult osteomalacia?
accept: Open epiphyseal growth plates fail to undergo provisional calcification and endochondral ossification
Rickets affects open growing epiphyseal cartilage plates

questions.q: Which characteristic chest wall deformity in rickets results from overgrowth and unmineralized widening of cartilage at the anterior costochondral junctions?
questions.explain: Palpable bead-like prominences along the costochondral junctions on the anterior chest wall constitute the rachitic rosary, often accompanied by Harrison sulcus along the diaphragmatic attachment.

open.q: Name the bead-like enlargements at the costochondral junctions classically seen in children with rickets.

questions.q: In chronic renal failure, renal osteodystrophy develops largely because damaged proximal renal tubular cells fail to express which enzyme required to produce active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol?
questions.explain: Renal proximal convoluted tubule cells house mitochondrial 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1), which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into active calcitriol; loss of this enzyme causes hypocalcaemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and renal osteodystrophy.

open.q: Name the renal proximal tubular enzyme lost in chronic kidney disease that normally converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into active calcitriol.

questions.q: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency causes scurvy primarily by impairing which post-translational enzymatic step during collagen biosynthesis?
options: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues on procollagen alpha chains
Cleavage of C-terminal propeptides by bone morphogenetic protein-1
Transcription of COL1A1 mRNA in the fibroblast nucleus
Glycosylation of fibronectin in the rough endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explain: Ascorbic acid keeps the iron cofactor of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in its active ferrous (Fe2+) state; without hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, procollagen cannot form stable triple helices or cross-links, causing fragile blood vessels and weak connective tissue.

open.q: Which specific biochemical step in collagen synthesis requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor?

questions.q: A 55-year-old man living alone on a tea-and-toast diet presents with swollen, spongy, bleeding gums, perifollicular petechiae, corkscrew hairs, and painful subperiosteal haemarthroses. Which vitamin deficiency explains his findings?
questions.explain: Scurvy results from dietary lack of fresh fruits and vegetables containing vitamin C, producing defective vascular basement membrane collagen with gingival bleeding, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, impaired wound healing, and subperiosteal haematomas.

open.q: Name the vitamin deficiency responsible for scurvy, presenting with bleeding spongy gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, and subperiosteal haematomas.

questions.sub: Vitamin E and Vitamin K Deficiencies
questions.q: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) protects polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes and lipoproteins primarily through which biochemical function?
options: Acting as a lipid-soluble chain-breaking free radical antioxidant
Serving as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase
Catalyzing oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids
Promoting intestinal active transport of dietary calcium
questions.explain: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant that scavenges lipid peroxyl radicals in cell membranes and myelin sheaths; severe deficiency (seen in abetalipoproteinaemia or chronic cholestasis) causes spinocerebellar ataxia and haemolytic anaemia.

open.q: What is the primary biochemical role of vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) in cellular membranes?
accept: Free radical scavenger preventing lipid peroxidation

questions.sub: Vitamin E and Vitamin K Deficiencies
questions.q: Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for hepatic gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which activates which group of coagulation factors and natural anticoagulants?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S
Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
Factors XI, XII, prekallikrein, and high-molecular-weight kininogen
von Willebrand factor and antithrombin III
questions.explain: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X as well as anticoagulant proteins C and S enables them to chelate calcium ions and bind negatively charged phospholipid membranes.

open.q: List the four procoagulant clotting factors that require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation for biological activity.
accept: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

questions.sub: Vitamin E and Vitamin K Deficiencies
questions.q: Why are exclusively breastfed newborn infants routinely administered intramuscular vitamin K at birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn?
options: Placental transfer is limited, breast milk is low in vitamin K and neonatal gut flora are immature
Neonatal hepatocytes lack vitamin K epoxide reductase for the first year
Maternal IgG destroys fetal factor VII
Placental vitamin K transfer causes fetal hypercoagulability
questions.explain: Vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly, breast milk is low in vitamin K, and the sterile newborn colon lacks menaquinone-producing commensal bacteria, placing unprophylaxed neonates at risk for intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeding.

open.q: Give two reasons why newborn infants are physiologically predisposed to vitamin K deficiency bleeding if not given prophylaxis at birth.
accept: Sterile gut lacking bacterial flora and low vitamin K in breast milk
Poor placental transfer, sterile neonatal gut, and low breast milk content

questions.q: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate and reduces transketolase activity, manifesting clinically as which three syndromes?
options: Dry beriberi, wet beriberi, and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis, and subacute combined degeneration
questions.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency impairs ATP generation in high-energy tissues, causing peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi), high-output dilated cardiomyopathy with oedema (wet beriberi), and haemorrhagic necrosis of mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey matter (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome).

open.q: Name the three major clinical syndromes caused by severe thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.
accept: Dry beriberi, wet beriberi, and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome

questions.q: At autopsy of a chronic alcoholic patient who presented with ophthalmoplegia, gait ataxia, and confabulation prior to death, symmetric petechial haemorrhages and atrophy are classically found in which brain structures?
options: Mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey matter
questions.explain: Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy is pathologically characterized by focal haemorrhage, endothelial proliferation, and gliosis symmetrically involving the mammillary bodies and walls of the third and fourth ventricles.

open.q: Which paired hypothalamic structures classically exhibit symmetric haemorrhage and atrophy at autopsy in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?

questions.q: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency produces pellagra, classically remembered by the 'three Ds' of dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia. Which dietary amino acid can be endogenously converted into niacin when vitamin B6 is sufficient?
questions.explain: Approximately 60 mg of dietary tryptophan can be converted to 1 mg of niacin; pellagra historically occurred in populations subsisting on untreated maize, where niacin is tightly bound (niacytin) and tryptophan content is low.

open.q: Name the essential dietary amino acid that serves as an endogenous precursor for niacin (vitamin B3) synthesis.

questions.q: Why does vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency cause subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord, whereas folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia without neurological disease?
options: B12 deficiency impairs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and myelin maintenance; folate deficiency primarily disrupts DNA synthesis
Folate crosses the BBB, whereas B12 cannot enter the CNS
B12 directly blocks intestinal pyridoxine absorption
Folate is required only by erythroblasts and not neurons
questions.explain: Both B12 and folate are required for methionine synthase and thymidylate/DNA synthesis (causing megaloblastic anaemia when either is deficient), but only B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; B12 deficiency accumulates methylmalonyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA, disrupting myelin synthesis.

open.q: Which vitamin B12-dependent mitochondrial enzyme fails in cobalamin deficiency, causing methylmalonic acid buildup and demyelinating spinal cord lesions not seen in folate deficiency?

questions.q: Which peripheral blood smear finding in polymorphonuclear neutrophils is an early, sensitive morphological hallmark of megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency?
options: Hypersegmented neutrophils (having 6 or more nuclear lobes)
questions.explain: Impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasmic growth, yielding macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (at least one neutrophil with >=6 lobes or >5% with 5 lobes).

open.q: Name the characteristic neutrophil nuclear abnormality seen on peripheral blood films in megaloblastic anaemia due to folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.q: Patients treated with isoniazid for tuberculosis frequently develop peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia unless supplemented with which vitamin?
questions.explain: Isoniazid forms inactive hydrazones with pyridoxal phosphate and increases renal pyridoxine excretion, impairing GABA synthesis (causing peripheral neuropathy) and delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase in haem synthesis (causing sideroblastic anaemia).

open.q: Name the B-complex vitamin depleted by isoniazid therapy, whose deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia.

questions.q: In Nigeria and worldwide, what is the single most common nutritional deficiency causing microcytic hypochromic anaemia?
questions.explain: Iron deficiency reduces haemoglobin synthesis within erythroid precursors, producing small pale erythrocytes (microcytic hypochromic anaemia), koilonychia (spoon nails), atrophic glossitis, and pica.

open.q: Name the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide that causes microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

questions.q: A 7-month-old infant weaned onto a zinc-poor diet presents with erythematous, crusted, eczematous plaques symmetrically distributed around the mouth, anus, and acral extremities, accompanied by alopecia and chronic diarrhoea. Which trace element deficiency causes this classic triad?
questions.explain: Zinc is a cofactor for over 300 metalloenzymes including DNA/RNA polymerases and alkaline phosphatase; deficiency (acquired or inherited acrodermatitis enteropathica due to ZIP4 mutation) produces periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhoea, and impaired wound healing.

open.q: Name the trace element whose deficiency produces the classic triad of periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhoea (acrodermatitis enteropathica).

questions.q: Endemic iodine deficiency leads to compensatory pituitary hypersecretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and diffuse follicular cell hyperplasia, manifesting clinically as what lesion?
questions.explain: Insufficient dietary iodine limits thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) synthesis, removing negative feedback on the pituitary; elevated TSH stimulates thyroid follicular hyperplasia and colloid accumulation (endemic goitre), and severe maternal deficiency causes congenital cretinism.

open.q: Name the compensatory thyroid enlargement resulting from TSH-driven follicular hyperplasia in populations with dietary iodine deficiency.

questions.q: Selenium serves as an essential component of selenocysteine in glutathione peroxidase and iodothyronine deiodinases. Severe dietary selenium deficiency in endemic regions causes which dilated cardiomyopathy in children and young women?
questions.explain: Keshan disease is an endemic congestive cardiomyopathy linked to severe selenium deficiency (and coxsackievirus cofactor) characterized by multifocal myocardial necrosis and replacement fibrosis.

open.q: Name the endemic dilated cardiomyopathy caused by severe dietary selenium deficiency.

questions.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification for adults, which body mass index (BMI) threshold defines obesity?
questions.explain: WHO defines normal adult BMI as 18.5-24.9 kg/m2, overweight (pre-obese) as 25.0-29.9 kg/m2, and obesity as BMI >= 30.0 kg/m2.

open.q: What minimum body mass index (BMI) threshold defines adult obesity according to the World Health Organization?

questions.q: Why does central (visceral/abdominal) obesity confer a significantly higher risk of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and atherosclerosis than gluteofemoral (subcutaneous) fat accumulation?
options: Visceral fat releases free fatty acids into portal blood and produces pro-inflammatory adipokines
Visceral fat secretes high levels of insulin-sensitising adiponectin
Subcutaneous fat lacks blood vessels and cannot store triglycerides
Visceral fat suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and VLDL production
questions.explain: Visceral adipose tissue drains into the portal circulation, flooding the liver with non-esterified free fatty acids (inducing hepatic insulin resistance and steatosis) and secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6, resistin) while reducing protective adiponectin.

open.q: Why is visceral (central) adiposity far more strongly linked to insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome than subcutaneous gluteofemoral fat?
accept: Portal release of free fatty acids and secretion of pro-inflammatory adipokines
Higher lipolytic activity draining into the portal vein and lower adiponectin secretion

questions.q: Which adipose-derived hormone acts on hypothalamic arcuate nucleus neurons to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure, and is paradoxically elevated in common human obesity due to central receptor resistance?
questions.explain: Leptin, encoded by the LEP (ob) gene and secreted in proportion to adipose mass, stimulates anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons and inhibits orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons; most obese individuals exhibit high circulating leptin with central leptin resistance.

open.q: Name the adipocyte-derived satiety hormone encoded by the ob gene that suppresses appetite via hypothalamic POMC neurons.

questions.q: Which orexigenic peptide hormone is secreted predominantly by neuroendocrine cells of the gastric fundus during fasting to stimulate appetite via hypothalamic NPY/AgRP neurons?
questions.explain: Ghrelin is the only known circulating appetite-stimulating (orexigenic) gut hormone; its levels peak just before meals and fall rapidly after food intake.

open.q: Name the appetite-stimulating peptide hormone secreted primarily by the stomach during fasting.

questions.q: Which beneficial adipokine is uniquely decreased in obesity and type 2 diabetes, normally acting through AMPK activation to enhance hepatic and skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity and exert anti-inflammatory effects?
questions.explain: Adiponectin is secreted exclusively by adipocytes; unlike other adipokines, its plasma concentration falls as fat mass expands, removing its insulin-sensitizing, fatty-acid-oxidizing, and anti-atherogenic protection.

open.q: Name the insulin-sensitizing, anti-inflammatory adipokine whose plasma levels characteristically decrease in obesity.

questions.q: High dietary consumption of smoked, salt-preserved, and nitrite-cured foods increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma primarily via endogenous intragastric formation of which carcinogenic compounds?
questions.explain: Dietary nitrites and nitrates used to cure meats and fish react with secondary amines in the acidic stomach (especially with hypochlorhydria and bacterial overgrowth) to form carcinogenic nitrosamines.

open.q: Name the carcinogenic compounds formed in the stomach from dietary nitrites and secondary amines in cured and smoked foods.

questions.q: High intake of red and processed meats combined with low dietary fibre intake is epidemiologically associated with an increased risk of which malignancy?
questions.explain: Low dietary fibre reduces stool bulk and slows intestinal transit, prolonging mucosal contact with secondary bile acids, haem-derived N-nitroso compounds, and heterocyclic amines generated from cooked red and processed meats.

open.q: Which gastrointestinal malignancy is strongly linked to diets high in red and processed meats and low in dietary fibre?

questions.q: Excessive chronic ingestion of which fat-soluble vitamin causes pseudotumour cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension), hepatomegaly with fibrosis, bone pain, and severe teratogenic craniofacial and cardiac malformations in pregnancy?
questions.explain: Fat-soluble vitamins A and D are stored in body tissues and cause severe toxicity when taken in excess; hypervitaminosis A produces headache/papilloedema (pseudotumour cerebri), dry desquamating skin, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity (contraindicating isotretinoin in pregnancy).

open.q: Name the fat-soluble vitamin whose excessive intake causes pseudotumour cerebri, hepatotoxicity, and severe fetal teratogenicity.

questions.q: Hypervitaminosis D leads to hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and metastatic calcification of blood vessels and soft tissues primarily by markedly increasing which physiological process?
options: Intestinal absorption of calcium and osteoclastic bone resorption
Renal tubular excretion of ionized calcium
Hepatic conjugation of bilirubin and bile salts
questions.explain: Excess active vitamin D metabolites super-stimulate intestinal calcium-binding protein (calbindin) expression and bone resorption, driving severe hypercalcaemia and metastatic calcification in renal tubules and arterial walls.

open.q: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which vitamin D toxicity produces metastatic calcification and nephrocalcinosis?
accept: Excessive intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption causing hypercalcaemia
